claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by the formation and dynamic integrity of a protective oxide film.
The governing protective film is notably a spinel-type oxide.
The protective oxide originates from surface enrichment of oxide-forming elements such as Al and Fe.
The oxide film acts as a diffusion barrier to aggressive ions and reduces direct metal attack.
Mechanical wear periodically disrupts the oxide film, after which the exposed metal re-oxidizes.
The balance between mechanical film removal and oxide reformation couples the wear and corrosion responses.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous multiphase or nanocrystalline high-entropy alloy without an intentionally pre-formed oxide.
Higher-temperature sintering or controlled pre-oxidation can induce surface enrichment and create a continuous protective oxide film.
The oxide film reduces exposed active-metal area, limits chloride transport, and slows anodic reactions.
Rapid film reformation after wear depends on the alloy chemistry.
Relative to a lower-temperature-processed baseline, the oxide-enriched alloy will have lower corrosion current density and higher passive-film resistance.
Relative to the baseline, the oxide-enriched alloy will have lower wear depth during tribo-corrosion.
Both the wear and corrosion components of total tribo-corrosion degradation will be lower in the oxide-enriched alloy.
A lower processing temperature or omission of pre-oxidation produces a patchy or weak oxide film and corrosion dominated by direct metal attack.
The protective effect will diminish when mechanical loading or chemical aggressiveness overwhelms oxide-reformation kinetics.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both corrosion and wear resistance, or failure to observe a continuous protective film, is proposed as grounds to reject the hypothesis.
